page_title: BBC Learning English - English at Work / Reality bites
title: Reality bites
topic: Language to use when making someone redundant
description:
At the offices of Tip Top Trading, the team is catching up on yesterday's good news from the conference. But today it's bad news that everyone is going to hear following Paul's chat with big boss, Mr Socrates. Someone is going to lose their job!
This episode focuses on the language that you might use or hear when someone in the company has to be made redundant.
phrases: We've got to move the furniture around.
I'm afraid I've got to let you go.
I'm giving you seven days' notice.

listening_challenge.question: What does Anna offer Denise to cry on?

transcript.speaker: Denise
transcript.text: Morning everyone. How did you get on at the conference?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Oh hi Denise. Yeah it was… it was OK.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: What do you mean 'OK'?  It was great. We made some new contacts and we won an award – Best Plastic Innovation of the Year, for our Imperial Lemon.

transcript.speaker: Denise
transcript.text: Oh that's wonderful. Wish I'd been there.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Maybe next year eh?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Maybe?Welcome back to the offices of Tip Top Trading where everyone is catching up on yesterday's good news. But today it's bad news that everyone is going to hear following Paul’s chat with the big boss, Mr Socrates. But how bad is it? Let's find out.

transcript.speaker: Paul
transcript.text: Morning everyone.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Hi Paul. Everything OK?

transcript.speaker: Paul
transcript.text: Yes, fine. Well done for winning Employee of the Year – I hope you can continue to be a great employee. Excuse me.

transcript.speaker: Denise
transcript.text: Hmm, he sounded odd. What did he mean?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Probably run out of biscuits!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: He's obviously got something on his mind.

transcript.speaker: Paul
transcript.text: Denise, could I have a word with you in my office please?

transcript.speaker: Denise
transcript.text: Of course. I'll bring my notepad and pen shall I?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: What's that all about? Anyway, now we're alone, I wanted to see what you're doing tonight… are you free?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Sorry Tom, I'm seeing Dave tonight. He's offered to fix something on my computer at home.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Oh, has he now?

transcript.speaker: Denise
transcript.text: All the years I've worked here – why me? Why now?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Denise, what's up?

transcript.speaker: Denise
transcript.text: Paul says he needs to move the furniture around and he has to let me go. He says he can't afford me anymore.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: That's terrible… but where's he letting you go to? And what furniture is he moving?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: No Anna! If someone says they are 'moving the furniture' they really mean they are restructuring or changing the business. And if they say 'they have to let you go', it means they are sacking you or in other words, ending your job.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Sacking you? Oh, that is serious. Denise, I'm really sorry to hear this. But why does Paul want to 'move the furniture' around?

transcript.speaker: Denise
transcript.text: He says it's because of the tough economic situation. My role is no longer needed

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Hey, that's not true. You make a great cup of tea Denise. I've got a good mind to smash Paul's bourbons into tiny crumbs. Grrr.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Calm down Tom. Now Denise, when did Paul say you had to go?

transcript.speaker: Denise
transcript.text: He's given me seven days' notice.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A 'notice period' is an amount of time an employer must give an employee if they plan to terminate their employment.

transcript.speaker: Denise
transcript.text: I never thought I would be facing redundancy… not now… not at my age.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Redundancy?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Yes, if someone says 'they are facing redundancy', it’s another way of saying they are losing their job. Hmm, I think Denise needs a shoulder to cry on.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Yes. Denise, do you want my shoulder to cry on?

transcript.speaker: Denise
transcript.text: Oh thanks.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Urgh! Erm… Denise, I've just made some tea would you like a cup?

transcript.speaker: Denise
transcript.text: Oh yes please.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Here you go. You know Denise, you've got to think positively. You'll get another job… and let's face it you didn't like working here anyway… you always looked so miserable.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: I don't think Tom's attempts to cheer Denise up are going to work! Losing your job can be a traumatic experience. It can come as a surprise and a shock. Let's hear the phrases Paul used to break the news to Denise:
We've got to move the furniture around.
I'm afraid I've got to let you go.
I'm giving you seven days' notice.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: And here are some other expressions you may hear in connection with losing your job:
Facing redundancy
Getting the sack
Terminating your employment
Leaving the company

transcript.speaker: Denise
transcript.text: Right, well, I might as well start clearing out my desk.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Yeah it's a real shame. Any chance I could have your stapler?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Tom, you could be a bit more sympathetic.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Oh right.

transcript.speaker: Paul
transcript.text: Tom, Anna. Could I have a word in my office please?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Oh no. This is it. It's my turn to get the chop!

transcript.speaker: Denise
transcript.text: Ha, You might not need my stapler after all!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Crikey! Things aren't looking good at Tip Top Trading. Are Tom and Anna getting the chop… I mean, the sack?  Join us again next time on English at Work.
